hero.title: UQ Connect
hero.sub: Rebuilding the information architecture of a student portal serving 50,000 students.

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Twelve top-level categories, most of them opaque.
ch.p: New students arrived at a portal written in staff-facing language — "HiQ", "SI-net", "mySI-net" — and had to guess. The search bar didn't forgive typos or synonyms. The mobile experience collapsed to a hamburger that hid 80+ links.

re.label: Research
re.title: Fifty students, three methods, one month.

m1.b: Open card sort on 42 common tasks.

m2.b: Task-based think-aloud on the live portal.

m3.b: Tree test, baseline vs. two alternatives.

re.quote: I just Google 'UQ how to drop a subject'. I never start on the portal.

sy.label: Synthesis
sy.title: The portal was organised by who owns the information, not who needs it.
sy.p: Affinity mapping revealed that student mental models clustered around five life-stages: arriving, studying, belonging, supporting myself, moving on. We collapsed twelve staff-oriented buckets into six task-oriented ones, with "I'm new" promoted to the front door.

id.label: IA decisions
id.p: Three alternative trees were tested; the winning one preserved a fallback alphabetical index for power users while leading with the task-first structure. Every category name went through a plain-language review with two non-UQ reviewers.

pr.label: Prototype
pr.p: A Figma prototype covered the top 15 tasks end-to-end at mid-fidelity. The navigation shell and the "I'm new" landing were built to high fidelity to validate reading flow on mobile.

te.label: Usability test
te.p: Eight students, moderated, remote. We found a naming collision between "Money" and "My account" that had only shown up at high fidelity — renamed on the spot; the re-run confirmed the fix.

ou.label: Outcome
ou.p: The redesigned IA is being adopted in phases by the UQ digital team. The tree test protocol and plain-language review have been reused on two subsequent university projects.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: The research phase was longer than planned — I would budget for that again. The most valuable decision was insisting on a plain-language review from non-UQ readers; it caught four category names that sounded fine to anyone steeped in the institution.

intro.p2: My approach combines analytical thinking with creative problem-solving. I believe that great design emerges from deeply understanding user needs and iterating towards solutions that are both functional and delightful.

headline.text: I make digital things people can actually find their way through.

about.p1: I'm finishing my Master of Interaction Design at the University of Queensland. Before that, I spent four years in a different discipline entirely, which is to say I got used to being the person in the room who has to translate between strangers.
about.p2: My work sits where research, architecture and craft overlap. I'm most useful on messy, high-stakes problems — the ones where nobody agrees what the product should be yet — because I enjoy the part everyone else finds tedious: reading interview transcripts at 1am until the pattern shows up.
about.p3: Outside the studio I cook with too much garlic, read non-fiction about cities, and occasionally attempt to learn Japanese. I reply to every email that isn't a recruiter mass-send.

1.b: If a study didn't change the design, the study wasn't necessary.

2.b: The best interaction is the one the user never notices solving their problem.

3.b: Empty states, errors, load states — that's where respect for the user lives.

4.b: A memo survives the meeting. A whiteboard doesn't.
